[2024 fall ms probability — problem 1]

$X$ has pmf $P(X=x) = c(2x+1)$ for $x = 0,1,2$. (1) Find $c$. (2) Compute $P(X=2)$. (3) $\mathbb{E}[X]$. (4) $\operatorname{Var}(X)$. (5) For 10 i.i.d. copies, find the distribution of the maximum. (6) Compute $P(\min(X_1,\dots,X_{10}) > 0)$.

From values c, 3c, and 5c, I calculate the sum as 9c, leading to c=1/9. Then, I find P2=5/9, E=13/9, and E[X^2]=23/9. The variance comes out to 38/81. response.text:
Let

\[
P(X=x)=c(2x+1), \qquad x=0,1,2.
\]

So the probabilities are

\[
P(X=0)=c,\qquad P(X=1)=3c,\qquad P(X=2)=5c.
\]

## (1) Find \(c\)

Since probabilities must sum to 1,

\[
c+3c+5c=1.
\]

Thus

\[
9c=1,
\]

so

\[
\boxed{c=\frac19}.
\]

## (2) Compute \(P(X=2)\)

\[
P(X=2)=c(2\cdot 2+1)=5c.
\]

Using \(c=1/9\),

\[
\boxed{P(X=2)=\frac59}.
\]

## (3) Compute \(\mathbb{E}[X]\)

\[
\mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_{x=0}^2 xP(X=x).
\]

Therefore,

\[
\mathbb{E}[X]
=0\cdot \frac19+1\cdot \frac39+2\cdot \frac59.
\]

So

\[
\mathbb{E}[X]=\frac39+\frac{10}{9}=\frac{13}{9}.
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{\mathbb{E}[X]=\frac{13}{9}}.
\]

## (4) Compute \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\)

We use

\[
\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb{E}[X^2]-\{\mathbb{E}[X]\}^2.
\]

First,

\[
\mathbb{E}[X^2]
=\sum_{x=0}^2 x^2P(X=x).
\]

Thus

\[
\mathbb{E}[X^2]
=0^2\cdot \frac19+1^2\cdot \frac39+2^2\cdot \frac59.
\]

So

\[
\mathbb{E}[X^2]
=\frac39+\frac{20}{9}
=\frac{23}{9}.
\]

Hence

\[
\operatorname{Var}(X)
=\frac{23}{9}-\left(\frac{13}{9}\right)^2.
\]

Compute:

\[
\operatorname{Var}(X)
=\frac{207}{81}-\frac{169}{81}
=\frac{38}{81}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{\operatorname{Var}(X)=\frac{38}{81}}.
\]

## (5) Distribution of the maximum of 10 i.i.d. copies

Let

\[
M=\max(X_1,\dots,X_{10}),
\]

where \(X_1,\dots,X_{10}\) are i.i.d. copies of \(X\).

The CDF of \(X\) is

\[
F(0)=P(X\le 0)=\frac19,
\]

\[
F(1)=P(X\le 1)=\frac19+\frac39=\frac49,
\]

\[
F(2)=1.
\]

For the maximum,

\[
P(M\le m)=P(X_1\le m,\dots,X_{10}\le m).
\]

By independence,

\[
P(M\le m)=F(m)^{10}.
\]

Thus the CDF of \(M\) is

\[
P(M\le m)=
\begin{cases}
0, & m<0,\\[4pt]
\left(\frac19\right)^{10}, & 0\le m<1,\\[4pt]
\left(\frac49\right)^{10}, & 1\le m<2,\\[4pt]
1, & m\ge 2.
\end{cases}
\]

Equivalently, the pmf of \(M\) is

\[
P(M=0)=\left(\frac19\right)^{10},
\]

\[
P(M=1)=\left(\frac49\right)^{10}-\left(\frac19\right)^{10},
\]

\[
P(M=2)=1-\left(\frac49\right)^{10}.
\]

So

\[
\boxed{
P(M=m)=
\begin{cases}
\left(\frac19\right)^{10}, & m=0,\\[4pt]
\left(\frac49\right)^{10}-\left(\frac19\right)^{10}, & m=1,\\[4pt]
1-\left(\frac49\right)^{10}, & m=2.
\end{cases}}
\]

## (6) Compute \(P(\min(X_1,\dots,X_{10})>0)\)

We need every \(X_i\) to be greater than 0. Since the \(X_i\) are independent,

\[
P(\min(X_1,\dots,X_{10})>0)
=P(X_1>0,\dots,X_{10}>0).
\]

Thus

\[
P(\min(X_1,\dots,X_{10})>0)
=\{P(X>0)\}^{10}.
\]

Now

\[
P(X>0)=P(X=1)+P(X=2)=\frac39+\frac59=\frac89.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{P(\min(X_1,\dots,X_{10})>0)=\left(\frac89\right)^{10}}.
\]
